title: NH: Less Transparency for Vouchers
author: Peter Greene
summary: New Hampshire's taxpayer-funded Education Freedom Accounts program is hiding spending details from public scrutiny. After journalist Jeremy Margolis exposed how ninety percent of tuition dollars went to religious schools and unusual expenses like ski lessons and equestrian classes, the Children's Scholarship Fund manager restricted the public database. Officials claimed this protects vendors from harassment, but the real effect is preventing taxpayers from seeing where their money goes. This opacity is a common feature of voucher programs with inadequate safeguards.
points: New Hampshire's voucher program hid spending data after journalists exposed ninety percent of tuition going to religious schools and extracurricular excess.
Officials claimed transparency restrictions protect vendors from harassment, but the effect prevents taxpayers from auditing their own education spending.
The program lacked basic safeguards before transparency was restricted, having no clear standards for vendor eligibility or reasonable spending limits.
Families spent over five hundred thousand dollars on extras like ski mountains, martial arts, and equestrian facilities using taxpayer vouchers.
Reducing transparency in voucher programs signals financial shenanigans and legislative irresponsibility by raising questions about what administrators fear exposing.
quotes: Turns out the New Hampshire taxpayer-funded voucher program would rather that people not be able to see details of how their money is spent. Were people really getting seven hundred fifty dollar piano lessons? Nope. They were buying pianos.
We learned that some individuals may have been misusing these reports to contact or harass small providers, or to question them about students and their activities.
This is baloney on a couple of levels. First, the state already has a full list of eligible vendors where voucher families can spend their pile of taxpayer dollars.
CSF has no business telling taxpayers and the press that they can't know where the money is going.

A voucher program that depends on operating with little or no transparency is waving a big fat red flag about financial shenanigans and legislative irresponsibility.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
